ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Subjects were primarily recruited from surrounding addiction medicine clinics.

> We enrolled 21 subjects maintained on SLB ≥1 year.

> Eleven subjects were prescribed films while ten were prescribed tablets.

> All participants completed and signed informed consent.

> Subjects completed a questionnaire assessing demographics, general medical history, dental history, oral hygiene practices, and dietary consumption.

> Thirty-one subjects were enrolled.

> Tablet subjects had a higher qualitative plaque level versus controls (p<0.05) (Table 1).

> Interestingly, tablet subjects had a higher DMFT and DMFS than film subjects, with more active carious surfaces extending into dentin or missing due to caries (p<0.05) (Fig. S1 and 1A).

> Most subjects were S. mutans positive, with no significant differences between groups (Fig. 1E).

> Of note, only four subjects in the control group had a carious lesion with sufficient plaque to collect, limiting carious plaque sample size.

> Importantly, 90-100% of SLB subjects were positive for C. albicans compared to only 10% of the controls (Fig. 1G).

> When participants were asked about dry mouth frequency, half of the SLB subjects reported often or always (Fig. 2B).

> All SLB subjects were categorized as having a low or very low buffering capacity (Fig. 2C).

> Because we recruited subjects that have been taking SLB for 1+ years, it is plausible that an initial rapid increase in DMFS occurred in tablet subjects that was not captured in this study.

> All tablet subjects had an elevated caries experience, with >75% of teeth on average affected, and thus may also explain why the tablet group appeared to already reach a plateau and therefore lacks a strong correlation in caries experience over time.

> Intriguingly, most SLB subjects were middle-aged yet still exhibited extremely high rates of S. mutans-C. albicans coinfection.

> While SLB does not appear to significantly impact flow rate, we found all SLB subjects had low or very low buffering capacity and lower baseline salivary pH, suggesting that buprenorphine, the excipients, or both may alter phosphate and bicarbonate buffering systems, thereby impairing neutralization and contributing to increased caries risk.

> A total of 31 subjects were enrolled.

Ethics approval statement:

> This cross-sectional clinical study was approved by the University of Florida Institutional Review Board (IRB202401848).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p<0.01", "p<0.05", 
"p<0.01", "p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p<0.01"), 
    Text = c("Results: Caries experience was greater in SLB subjects than controls and higher among tablet versus film subjects (p<0.05).", 
    "SLB subjects exhibited lower salivary pH and buffering capacity (p<0.05), and elevated salivary levels of Mutans streptococci (p<0.05) and Candida spp.", 
    "Salivary buprenorphine exposure was elevated and correlated with baseline pH (p<0.01), suggesting ion trapping contributes to oral retention.", 
    "Participants taking films or tablets were more likely to use tobacco than the controls (p<0.05), and subjects taking tablets were also more likely to have previously used cannabis (p<0.01) or other non-opioid illicit substances (p<0.01) versus controls (Table 1).", 
    "Participants taking films or tablets were more likely to use tobacco than the controls (p<0.05), and subjects taking tablets were also more likely to have previously used cannabis (p<0.01) or other non-opioid illicit substances (p<0.01) versus controls (Table 1).", 
    "The only significant difference between film and tablet groups was prior cannabis use (p<0.05).", 
    "Tablet subjects had a higher qualitative plaque level versus controls (p<0.05) (Table 1).", 
    "The DMFT and DMFS were significantly higher in both SLB groups relative to controls (p<0.05) (Fig. S1 & Fig. 1A).", 
    "Interestingly, tablet subjects had a higher DMFT and DMFS than film subjects, with more active carious surfaces extending into dentin or missing due to caries (p<0.05) (Fig. S1 and 1A).", 
    "Furthermore, baseline pH of both saliva and carious plaque in film and tablet subjects was lower than controls (p<0.01) (Fig. 2D)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.14", "p=0.07", "p=0.14", "p=0.07" ), Sentence = c("The tablet group mean area under pH5.7 and time under pH5.7 from plaque was over 3-fold and 4-fold higher than the film group, respectively, although this difference was not significant (p=0.14) (Fig. S2A-B).", "The mean area and time under pH6.2 followed a similar trend (Fig. S2C-D), and the minimum plaque pH trended lower in tablet subjects relative to those using films (p=0.07) (Fig. S2E).", "Additionally, acid exposure trended higher in plaque from tablet subjects (p=0.14) and the minimum plaque pH trended lower (p=0.07).", "Additionally, acid exposure trended higher in plaque from tablet subjects (p=0.14) and the minimum plaque pH trended lower (p=0.07)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

summary_table.ethics_statements: This cross-sectional clinical study was approved by the University of Florida Institutional Review Board (IRB202401848).
live_data_statements: Subjects were primarily recruited from surrounding addiction medicine clinics.
We enrolled 21 subjects maintained on SLB ≥1 year.
Eleven subjects were prescribed films while ten were prescribed tablets.
All participants completed and signed informed consent.
Subjects completed a questionnaire assessing demographics, general medical history, dental history, oral hygiene practices, and dietary consumption.
Tablet subjects had a higher qualitative plaque level versus controls (p<0.05) (Table 1).
Interestingly, tablet subjects had a higher DMFT and DMFS than film subjects, with more active carious surfaces extending into dentin or missing due to caries (p<0.05) (Fig. S1 and 1A).
Most subjects were S. mutans positive, with no significant differences between groups (Fig. 1E).
Of note, only four subjects in the control group had a carious lesion with sufficient plaque to collect, limiting carious plaque sample size.
Importantly, 90-100% of SLB subjects were positive for C. albicans compared to only 10% of the controls (Fig. 1G).
When participants were asked about dry mouth frequency, half of the SLB subjects reported often or always (Fig. 2B).
All SLB subjects were categorized as having a low or very low buffering capacity (Fig. 2C).
Because we recruited subjects that have been taking SLB for 1+ years, it is plausible that an initial rapid increase in DMFS occurred in tablet subjects that was not captured in this study.

All tablet subjects had an elevated caries experience, with >75% of teeth on average affected, and thus may also explain why the tablet group appeared to already reach a plateau and therefore lacks a strong correlation in caries experience over time.
Intriguingly, most SLB subjects were middle-aged yet still exhibited extremely high rates of S. mutans-C. albicans coinfection.

While SLB does not appear to significantly impact flow rate, we found all SLB subjects had low or very low buffering capacity and lower baseline salivary pH, suggesting that buprenorphine, the excipients, or both may alter phosphate and bicarbonate buffering systems, thereby impairing neutralization and contributing to increased caries risk.
A total of 31 subjects were enrolled.
